topics.name: Number and Algebra
topics.title: IB Math AA SL Number and Algebra: Syllabus Guide and Examples
topics.description: Study the IB Mathematics AA SL Number and Algebra syllabus with a topic checklist, clear explanations, worked examples, and original practice with answers.
keywords: IB Math AA SL number and algebra
IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches sequences
IB Math AA SL binomial theorem
topics.intro: Number and Algebra connects number representation, patterns, financial growth, exponents, logarithms, proof and expansion. This guide follows the current AA SL syllabus first assessed in 2021; it is not the 2029 course guide.
coverage: 1.4 Financial applications and geometric sequences and series
1.5 Integer exponents and introduction to logarithms
1.7 Rational exponents and laws of logarithms
1.8 Sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences
1.9 Binomial theorem for a natural number exponent

sections.title: Standard form and sensible precision
points: Write a non-zero number as a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ |a| < 10 and n is an integer. Normalize the leading number after multiplying or dividing so it returns to the required range.

When a result describes a measurement or estimate, keep precision consistent with the information given. A calculator display does not by itself determine the appropriate number of significant figures.

sections.title: Arithmetic and geometric sequences
points: An arithmetic sequence has a constant difference d: uₙ = u₁ + (n − 1)d. Its first n terms sum to Sₙ = n/2[2u₁ + (n − 1)d].
A geometric sequence has a constant ratio r: uₙ = u₁rⁿ⁻¹. For r ≠ 1, Sₙ = u₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r). The order of terms matters: identify u₁, d or r before substituting.
A repeated percentage change is geometric. If an amount P grows by rate i each period, its value after n periods is P(1 + i)ⁿ. Depreciation by rate i uses P(1 − i)ⁿ.

sections.title: Exponents and logarithms
points: For positive bases, use aᵐaⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. Rational exponents give roots, for example a¹ᐟ² = √a when the real square root is defined.

A logarithm answers an exponential question: logₐx = y means aʸ = x, with a > 0, a ≠ 1 and x > 0. The product, quotient and power laws are logₐ(xy) = logₐx + logₐy, logₐ(x/y) = logₐx − logₐy and logₐ(xᵏ) = k logₐx.
Check the domain before accepting a logarithmic solution. The argument of each real logarithm must be positive.

sections.title: Proof, infinite sums and the binomial theorem
points: A simple proof uses a valid definition or known result to establish a statement for every permitted value. State the domain and show the logical step; several confirming examples do not prove a general claim.
An infinite geometric series converges only when |r| < 1. Its sum is S∞ = u₁/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, this formula does not give a finite sum.
For a natural number n, (a + b)ⁿ = Σᵣ₌₀ⁿ (ⁿCᵣ)aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ. Each coefficient comes from the binomial coefficient, and the exponents in every term add to n.

examples.title: Find a term and a partial sum
examples.question: An arithmetic sequence begins 7, 11, 15, … Find u₁₂ and the sum of the first 12 terms.
steps: The first term is u₁ = 7 and the common difference is d = 4.

examples.title: Model compound growth
examples.question: ₹5,000 is invested at 4% compound interest per year. Find its value after 3 years, to the nearest rupee.
steps: The growth factor per year is 1 + 0.04 = 1.04.
Round only at the end because the question asks for the nearest rupee.

examples.title: Solve an exponential equation
examples.question: Solve 3²ˣ⁻¹ = 27.
steps: The bases are equal and positive, so 2x − 1 = 3.

practice.question: An arithmetic sequence has u₁ = 9 and d = 5. Find u₂₀ and S₂₀.
Find the sum to infinity of 12 + 6 + 3 + … .
Expand (x + 2)³.
practice.solution: Using the binomial coefficients 1, 3, 3, 1 gives x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

commonMistakes: Using n rather than n − 1 in the nth-term formula.
Applying the infinite-sum formula without checking |r| < 1.
Treating log(a + b) as log a + log b; the product law applies to log(ab), not a sum inside the logarithm.
Rounding intermediate values in a financial model and accumulating avoidable error.
revision: Can I identify whether a sequence is arithmetic or geometric and justify the choice?
Can I select the nth-term or sum formula that matches the question?
Can I solve exponential and logarithmic equations while checking restrictions?
Can I explain why an infinite geometric series converges before finding its sum?

topics.name: Functions
topics.title: IB Math AA SL Functions: Syllabus Guide and Worked Examples
topics.description: Review the IB Math AA SL Functions syllabus, including graphs, transformations, quadratics, inverses, and original practice with worked answers.
topics.intro: Functions describe how inputs map to outputs and how relationships appear in equations, tables and graphs. This guide covers all current AA SL Functions syllabus points and uses original examples.
coverage: 2.1 Gradients and equations of straight lines
2.7 Solving quadratic equations and inequalities; the discriminant

sections.title: Inputs, outputs and domain
points: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. Use function notation such as f(3) to mean the output when the input is 3.

The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of resulting outputs. For rational functions, exclude inputs that make a denominator zero. For real logarithmic functions, require a positive argument.
A straight line with gradient m through (x₁, y₁) can be written y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). A graph communicates solutions and key features, but an algebraic method can give exact values.

sections.title: Compositions, identity and inverse functions
points: A composite function applies one function after another: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)). The order matters; f(g(x)) is not generally equal to g(f(x)).
The identity function maps x to x. An inverse reverses the mapping: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x on the appropriate domain. To find an inverse, write y = f(x), swap x and y, then solve for y.
A function must be one-to-one on the chosen domain to have an inverse that is itself a function. Graphically, it must pass the horizontal-line test.

sections.title: Quadratics and other graph families
points: A quadratic can be read in expanded form ax² + bx + c, factorized form a(x − p)(x − q), or vertex form a(x − h)² + k. These forms reveal different features of the same function.
The discriminant Δ = b² − 4ac determines the number of distinct real roots: positive gives two, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives no real roots.
Reciprocal and rational functions can have excluded inputs and asymptotes. Exponential and logarithmic functions are inverses; their graphs reflect across y = x when domains and ranges are matched.

A transformation such as y = f(x − h) + k shifts the graph h units horizontally and k units vertically. A negative multiplier outside the function reflects it in the x-axis; a negative inside reflects it in the y-axis.

sections.title: Solving graphically and analytically
points: An intersection of y = f(x) and y = g(x) solves f(x) = g(x). Read an approximate solution from a graph when appropriate; use algebra when an exact solution is required and available.
Label axes and important points clearly when drawing or sketching. A sketch should show the features needed to communicate the function, such as intercepts, turning points and asymptotes.

examples.title: Read a quadratic in vertex form
examples.question: For f(x) = (x − 2)² − 3, state the vertex, axis of symmetry and roots.
steps: The form (x − h)² + k gives vertex (h, k), so the vertex is (2, −3).
The axis of symmetry is x = 2.

examples.title: Solve a quadratic inequality
examples.question: Solve x² − 4 ≤ 0.
steps: Factor: (x − 2)(x + 2) ≤ 0. The critical values are −2 and 2.
The parabola opens upward, so it is at or below the x-axis between the roots, including both roots.

practice.question: Find the gradient of the line through (−1, 4) and (3, 12), then write its equation.
For g(x) = −(x + 1)² + 4, give the vertex and maximum value.
practice.solution: The vertex form gives vertex (−1, 4). The negative coefficient makes it open downward, so the maximum value is 4.

practice.question: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 and state the discriminant.
practice.solution: Factor to (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, giving x = 2 or 3. The discriminant is 25 − 24 = 1, so there are two distinct real roots.

commonMistakes: Confusing f⁻¹(x), the inverse function, with 1/f(x), the reciprocal.
Changing the sign incorrectly in a horizontal transformation: f(x − h) shifts right by h.
Giving a root without checking whether it satisfies a domain restriction.
Using a graph estimate where the question asks for an exact answer, or giving too many digits for an approximate answer.
revision: Can I move between a function rule, a table and a labelled graph?
Can I identify domain, range, intercepts, turning points and asymptotes where relevant?
Can I compose functions and find an inverse on a stated domain?
Can I explain whether an equation has zero, one or two real roots using the discriminant?

topics.name: Geometry and Trigonometry
topics.title: IB Math AA SL Geometry and Trigonometry: Syllabus Guide
topics.description: Study IB Math AA SL Geometry and Trigonometry with the current syllabus checklist, radians, exact values, identities, worked examples, and practice.
keywords: IB Math AA SL geometry and trigonometry
topics.intro: Geometry and Trigonometry links diagrams, angle measure, circle properties and trigonometric functions. Sketch carefully, label known information and choose a relation that matches the geometry.
coverage: 3.5 Definitions, exact values and the ambiguous case of the sine rule
3.7 Functions and transformations of sine, cosine and tangent
3.8 Solving trigonometric equations graphically and analytically

sections.title: Diagrams, triangles and circle measure
points: A clear diagram helps distinguish a given length or angle from an unknown. Mark right angles, equal lengths and angle labels before selecting a formula.

In a right-angled triangle, use sine, cosine and tangent with the correct opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse sides. For a non-right triangle, the sine rule relates side lengths to opposite angles; the cosine rule relates all three sides and an included angle.
Radians measure angles by arc length divided by radius. For θ in radians, arc length s = rθ and sector area A = ½r²θ. Use radians in these formulae.

sections.title: Exact trigonometric values and identities
points: Know the exact sine, cosine and tangent values for standard angles and use the unit circle to determine signs in each quadrant.
The identity sin²x + cos²x = 1 connects sine and cosine. Other relationships follow by dividing by sin²x or cos²x when the expressions are defined.
The sine rule can have two possible angles in the ambiguous case because sin B = sin(180° − B). Use the triangle angle sum and the given side information to decide which candidates are valid.

sections.title: Trigonometric graphs and equations
points: The graphs of y = sin x and y = cos x repeat every 2π radians; y = tan x repeats every π and has vertical asymptotes where it is undefined.

For y = a sin(b(x − c)) + d, the amplitude is |a|, the period is 2π/|b|, the horizontal shift is c and the vertical shift is d. Read the equation and graph together rather than relying on appearance alone.

When solving a trigonometric equation, state the interval, find all solutions in that interval and use the period and symmetry to avoid missing roots. A graphical solution may be approximate; an analytical solution can be exact.

examples.title: Find an arc length and sector area
examples.question: A circle has radius 6 cm and a sector angle of 5π/6 radians. Find the arc length and area of the sector.

examples.title: Check the ambiguous case of the sine rule
examples.question: In a triangle, a = 8 is opposite A = 30° and b = 12 is opposite B. Find the possible values of B.
steps: By the sine rule, sin B / 12 = sin 30° / 8, so sin B = 0.75.
The calculator gives B ≈ 48.6°. The second angle with the same sine is 180° − 48.6° = 131.4°.
Both fit with A = 30° because each leaves a positive angle for the third vertex.

examples.title: Solve a trigonometric equation on an interval
examples.question: Solve 2 sin x = √3 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
steps: The reference angle is π/3 and sine is positive in quadrants I and II.
The solutions in the requested interval are π/3 and 2π/3.

practice.question: A sector has radius 4 cm and angle 1.2 radians. Find its arc length and area.
Solve cos x = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
practice.solution: Cosine is 1/2 at reference angle π/3 in quadrants I and IV, so x = π/3 or 5π/3.

practice.question: A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. Find the other leg and the acute angle opposite the leg of length 5.
practice.solution: The other leg is √(13² − 5²) = 12. The angle satisfies sin θ = 5/13, so θ ≈ 22.6°.

commonMistakes: Using degrees in s = rθ or A = ½r²θ instead of radians.
Using the sine rule with a side and a non-opposite angle.
Returning only the principal inverse-trigonometric value and missing other solutions in the interval.
Leaving off units for a length or area.
revision: Can I choose between right-triangle ratios, the sine rule and the cosine rule?
Can I convert between degrees and radians and use circle formulae with radians?
Can I use exact values, identities and quadrant signs to solve equations?
Can I find every solution within a stated interval?

topics.name: Statistics and Probability
topics.title: IB Math AA SL Statistics and Probability: Syllabus Guide
topics.description: Review the IB Math AA SL Statistics and Probability syllabus with data summaries, probability, distributions, normal z-values, worked examples, and practice.
keywords: IB Math AA SL statistics and probability
topics.intro: Statistics describes and models data; probability quantifies uncertainty. Interpret results in context, state assumptions and distinguish association from causation.
coverage: 4.2 Presenting data with tables, histograms and cumulative frequency
4.3 Measures of central tendency and dispersion
4.6 Diagrams, conditional probability, combined and independent events
4.10 Equation of the regression line of x on y
4.11 Formulae for conditional probabilities and independent events

sections.title: Sampling, displays and summary statistics
points: A sample should represent the population relevant to the question. A convenience sample may be biased even when it is large; describe how data were selected before drawing conclusions.

Tables, histograms and cumulative-frequency displays organize data differently. In a histogram with unequal class widths, compare frequency density (frequency divided by class width), not bar height alone.

The mean uses every value and is sensitive to extremes; the median is resistant to extreme values. Measures of spread such as the interquartile range and standard deviation describe variability, so report a suitable centre and spread together.

sections.title: Correlation, regression and probability
points: A correlation coefficient summarizes the strength and direction of a linear relationship. Correlation does not establish that one variable causes the other.
The regression line of y on x predicts y from x; the regression line of x on y predicts x from y. These are different fits and should be used for the variable being predicted.
For events A and B, P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), provided P(B) > 0. Independence means P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A|B) = P(A) when defined.
Tree diagrams, Venn diagrams and tables help keep conditional and combined probabilities organized. Label branches with conditional probabilities where appropriate.

sections.title: Random variables and distributions
points: A discrete random variable X takes countable values with probabilities that sum to 1. Its expectation is E(X) = ΣxP(X = x), a long-run average rather than a promise about one trial.
A binomial model requires a fixed number n of independent trials, two outcomes per trial and a constant success probability p. Then P(X = k) = ⁿCₖpᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ.
A normal model is described by its mean μ and standard deviation σ. Standardize x using z = (x − μ)/σ, then use the normal distribution or the permitted calculator function to find probabilities.

examples.title: Find a binomial probability
examples.question: A component is defective with probability 0.1, independently for each component. In a sample of 5, find the probability that exactly one is defective.
steps: X is binomial with n = 5 and p = 0.1 because the trials are independent and p is constant.

examples.title: Standardize a normal value
examples.question: A normal variable has mean 70 and standard deviation 8. Find the z-value for x = 82.
examples.answer: The value 82 is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.

examples.title: Use conditional probability
examples.question: In a group, 60% study French, 40% study Spanish, and 25% study both. Find P(French | Spanish).

practice.question: A fair coin is tossed 6 times. Find the probability of exactly 4 heads.
Exam scores are modelled by N(68, 10²). Find the z-value for a score of 83.
If P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4 and A and B are independent, find P(A ∩ B) and P(A | B).
practice.solution: P(A ∩ B) = 0.3(0.4) = 0.12. Independence gives P(A | B) = P(A) = 0.3.

commonMistakes: Assuming correlation proves a causal relationship.
Using the regression line in the wrong direction for the variable being predicted.
Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A).
Applying a binomial model when trials are dependent or the probability changes.
Using σ rather than σ² in a calculator field that asks for variance.
revision: Can I explain whether a sample is likely to represent its population?
Can I choose an appropriate centre and spread and interpret them in context?
Can I distinguish correlation, regression and causation?
Can I identify when a binomial or normal model is appropriate and interpret calculator output?

topics.name: Calculus
topics.title: IB Math AA SL Calculus: Syllabus Guide and Worked Examples
topics.description: Learn the IB Math AA SL Calculus syllabus: limits, derivatives, tangents, optimization, kinematics, integrals, areas, worked examples, and practice.
keywords: IB Math AA optimization and kinematics
topics.intro: Calculus studies how quantities change and accumulate. Derivatives describe instantaneous rates of change; definite integrals measure signed accumulation over an interval.
coverage: 5.8 Maximum, minimum and inflection points; optimization
5.10 Indefinite integrals, including inspection and substitution
5.11 Definite integrals and area under and between curves

sections.title: Limits, derivatives and gradients
points: The derivative f′(x) is the limiting gradient of a secant as its two points approach one another. At a point where f is differentiable, f′(x) is the gradient of the tangent and the instantaneous rate of change.
For f(x) = axⁿ, f′(x) = anxⁿ⁻¹. Use the product, chain and quotient rules when the expression is a product, a composite or a quotient of functions.
A tangent with gradient m at (a, f(a)) has equation y − f(a) = m(x − a). A normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient is −1/m when m ≠ 0.

sections.title: Monotonicity and stationary points
points: Where f′(x) > 0, the function is increasing; where f′(x) < 0, it is decreasing. Solve f′(x) = 0 to find stationary points, then use sign changes or the second derivative to classify them.
The second derivative f″ describes how the gradient changes. A change in concavity may indicate an inflection point, but check the function’s behaviour around the candidate value.
For optimization, define the quantity to optimize, express it in one variable, state any domain restrictions, find critical points and test which value gives the required maximum or minimum.

sections.title: Integrals and accumulation
points: An indefinite integral reverses differentiation and includes a constant: ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C where F′(x) = f(x). Substitution can simplify a composite expression by replacing its inner function with a new variable.

A definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx is signed area. For geometric area below the x-axis, reverse the sign; for area between curves, integrate upper function minus lower function over intervals where their order is fixed.

The trapezoidal rule estimates area from equally spaced ordinates; it is an approximation. In kinematics, if s(t) is position, v(t) = s′(t) and a(t) = v′(t). Track units and distinguish displacement from distance travelled.

examples.title: Classify stationary points
examples.question: For f(x) = x³ − 3x, find and classify the stationary points.
steps: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1), so stationary points occur at x = −1 and x = 1.
At x = −1, f″(−1) < 0, giving a local maximum (−1, 2). At x = 1, f″(1) > 0, giving a local minimum (1, −2).

examples.title: Find a tangent and normal
examples.question: Find the tangent and normal to y = x² + 1 at x = 2.
steps: The point is (2, 5). The derivative is dy/dx = 2x, so the tangent gradient is 4.
The normal gradient is −1/4. Normal: y − 5 = −¼(x − 2).

examples.title: Integrate by substitution and evaluate
examples.question: Evaluate ∫₀¹ 2x(x² + 1)³ dx.
steps: Let u = x² + 1, so du = 2x dx. When x = 0, u = 1; when x = 1, u = 2.

practice.question: Find the stationary point of f(x) = x² − 6x + 5 and classify it.
practice.solution: f′(x) = 2x − 6 = 0 gives x = 3. f(3) = −4 and f″(x) = 2 > 0, so the point (3, −4) is a minimum.

practice.question: Find the area between y = 4 and y = x² from x = 0 to x = 2.
practice.solution: On this interval 4 ≥ x². Area = ∫₀²(4 − x²)dx = [4x − x³/3]₀² = 8 − 8/3 = 16/3 square units.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the chain-rule factor from the inner function.
Calling every solution of f′(x) = 0 a maximum or minimum without checking the behaviour.
Using the same gradient for the tangent and normal; perpendicular non-vertical lines have gradients whose product is −1.
Treating a definite integral as unsigned geometric area when the curve is below the axis.
Omitting the constant of integration from an indefinite integral.
revision: Can I interpret a derivative as a gradient or rate in context?
Can I choose and apply the power, product, chain or quotient rule?
Can I classify stationary points and set up an optimization model?
Can I distinguish signed integral, geometric area, displacement and distance?

comparison.title: IB Math AA vs AI: Differences, Assessment and How to Choose
comparison.description: Compare IB Mathematics AA and AI: course focus, technology, assessment and questions to ask before choosing SL or HL.
keywords: IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches vs Applications and Interpretation
which IB maths should I choose
IB AA or AI SL HL difference
comparison.intro: IB Diploma Programme Mathematics has two courses, Analysis and Approaches (AA) and Applications and Interpretation (AI), each offered at Standard Level (SL) and Higher Level (HL). They develop related mathematics through different emphases. Neither course is universally easier or the right choice for every student.

rows.aa: Algebraic methods, mathematical structure, reasoning and analysis of functions and calculus.
rows.ai: Mathematical modelling, statistics, interpretation of results and applications in context.

rows.aa: Manipulating expressions, constructing arguments, analysing functions and solving abstract or contextual problems.
rows.ai: Choosing a model, using data and technology, interpreting outputs, and evaluating whether a result makes sense in context.

rows.aa: For the current syllabus, Paper 1 is completed without technology and Paper 2 uses technology. HL also has Paper 3.
rows.ai: For the current syllabus, technology is required in the external papers. HL also has Paper 3.

rows.aa: Both courses include an individual Mathematical Exploration.
rows.ai: Both courses include an individual Mathematical Exploration.

rows.aa: Do I enjoy symbolic work, algebraic reasoning and following a solution without a calculator?
rows.ai: Do I enjoy data, modelling, technology-supported investigation and interpreting results in context?

guidance: Start with the mathematics you enjoy and the way you prefer to solve problems. A course label alone does not predict the grade you will earn.

Check entry requirements for the specific university programmes you may apply to. Requirements vary by country, institution, course and year; do not rely on a blanket rule that AA or AI is always accepted or required.
Discuss your choice with your IB mathematics teacher or school coordinator, especially if you are deciding between SL and HL or balancing your other Diploma Programme subjects.
Do not choose based only on which course is said to be easier. AA and AI emphasize different kinds of reasoning and both require consistent practice.
comparison.assessment: In the current syllabus, SL students sit two external papers and complete the Mathematical Exploration. HL students sit three external papers and complete the exploration. Paper formats and technology rules differ between AA and AI; check the subject guide for the examination session you will take. The current syllabus has its final assessment in November 2028, before the new curriculum is first assessed in 2029.

faq.question: Is IB Math AA harder than AI?
faq.answer: There is no universal answer. AA puts more weight on algebraic reasoning and analysis; AI puts more weight on modelling, statistics, technology and interpretation. Difficulty depends on a student's strengths and preparation.

faq.question: Can AI lead to a STEM degree?
faq.answer: Some STEM programmes accept AI and others specify a course or level. Requirements vary, so check the current admissions page for each programme you are considering.

faq.question: Do AA and AI both have SL and HL?
faq.answer: Yes. Both courses are offered at Standard Level and Higher Level. Students take one DP Mathematics course.
